citeAs: Bisk, Y., Zellers, R., Le Bras, R., Gao, J., and Choi, Y. (2020). PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language. AAAI.
creator: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi (Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Microsoft Research AI, Carnegie Mellon University, University of Washington)
description: PIQA is a benchmark dataset for physical commonsense reasoning in natural language. It consists of multiple-choice questions where a model must select the most sensible solution to a physical goal from two options. The dataset contains over 16,000 training QA pairs with additional development and test sets, inspired by instructables.com and designed to test knowledge of physical properties, affordances, and object manipulation.
name: PIQA (Physical Interaction: Question Answering)
rai:annotationsPerItem: Each item was validated by multiple annotators; examples with low inter-annotator agreement were removed. Human performance was calculated by majority vote among annotators who achieved 90% on the qualification HIT.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotators were Amazon Mechanical Turk workers who passed a qualification HIT requiring >80% accuracy. Annotator pay averaged >$15/hr according to self-reporting on turkerview.com and timing calculations. No further demographic information (age, gender, nationality, language background) is provided.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Examples with low annotator agreement during validation were removed from the dataset. Human performance was evaluated on the development set using majority vote among annotators who had achieved 90% accuracy on the qualification HIT, yielding 94.9% accuracy.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were shown an instructable page and asked to provide: (1) a physical goal, (2) a valid solution, and (3) a "trick" — a subtly incorrect solution that sounds reasonable but is wrong due to a subtle misunderstanding of preconditions or physics. A qualification HIT was required before participation, where annotators had to achieve >80% accuracy identifying well-formed vs. underspecified (goal, solution) pairs. Data was collected in batches and validated by other annotators. A diff button was provided in the interface to highlight differences between solutions. Examples with low agreement during validation were removed. Annotator pay averaged >$15/hr.
rai:dataBiases: Reporting bias was identified as a major concern: when thinking about how to achieve a goal, people are drawn to prototypical solutions and common tools (e.g., kitchen utensils, garage tools), rarely considering the full range of everyday objects. To address this, annotators were prompted with instructables links to encourage atypical solutions and flatten the distribution of referenced objects. Annotation artifacts (stylistic biases that artificially inflate model performance) were removed using the AFLite algorithm. The dataset was specifically constructed to be adversarial to BERT to avoid trivial solutions.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected via Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) HITs. Annotators were prompted with links to instructables.com pages (covering six categories: costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop) and asked to: (1) construct a physical goal, (2) provide a valid solution, and (3) provide a "trick" — a subtly incorrect solution that sounds plausible. Two examples were drawn per instructable. Data was collected in batches of several thousand triples and validated by other annotators for correctness. Users with low agreement were de-qualified.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Instructions and goals sourced from instructables.com, a crowdsourced collection of instructions for activities including cooking, car repair, crafting, and home projects. Annotators used these as inspiration to construct goal-solution pairs.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping, Crowdsourcing
rai:dataLimitations: Examples requiring expert-level domain knowledge (e.g., special woodworking terminology) were removed during validation as they fall outside "commonsense." The dataset focuses on physical commonsense and may not generalize to other types of commonsense reasoning. Models trained on large web crawls may eventually surpass human performance by finding in-domain data, which the authors note is not the intended use. Physical commonsense knowledge is inherently limited in text due to reporting bias.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The AFLite algorithm was applied to remove annotation artifacts and spurious biases. AFLite fine-tunes BERT-Large on 5,000 examples to compute embeddings of all remaining instances, then uses an ensemble of linear classifiers trained on random subsets to identify instances whose embeddings are highly indicative of the correct answer label. Such instances are discarded. Train, development, and test folds were automatically produced by AFLite. Text was tokenized using Spacy and the GPT BPE tokenizer for analysis. Examples were truncated at 150 tokens during model evaluation (affecting ~1% of data).
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance AI systems' understanding of physical commonsense, which is critical for building language models useful beyond NLP — including robots that interact with the world and understand natural language. The authors argue that knowledge should ultimately be learned from interaction with the world rather than language alone, and PIQA is intended to highlight this gap and motivate future research.
rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking progress in physical commonsense understanding for natural language understanding models. Probing and diagnosing the physical knowledge encoded in large pretrained language models. Advancing language representations that capture physical world knowledge for applications in robotics and embodied AI.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: AFLite algorithm (using BERT-Large fine-tuned on 5,000 examples) was used to identify and remove annotation artifacts. Spacy was used for tokenization and part-of-speech tagging. GPT BPE tokenizer was used for sequence length analysis.
